div.p: Many real-time systems have timing requirements that are dificult to fulfil i f the system i s implemented by software running on a microprocessor. One way to remedy this problem is to implement the most timecritical parts in application-specific integrated circuits instead. Hardware/software codesign aims at providing support for the designer of such a heterogeneously implemented system, and especially at finding ways to determine what parts should be implemented in what technology. In this paper, we discuss an approach to codesign which has as its objective to find an implementation of a real-time system, which allows the deadlines to be met. The main result presented is a schedulability evaluation method, and we describe how this can be used to guide the partitioning of the system behaviour onto the different components of a hardware architecture.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The field of hardwarelsoftware codesign (or simply codesign, for short) has received increasing attention during the last few years, and many different aspects have been treated in numerous publications. Much of the early work on codesign had the objective of achieving a maximal increase in execution speed as compared to a pure software implementation, and it is only recently that some attention has been given to codesign of embedded real-time systems [4,6, 121. This is somewhat surprising, since this application area is one of those for which codesign is best suited, for the following reasons: 0 We normally have fairly exact requirements on the capacity and timing of a real-time system, and it is therefore more important to make exactly the right choice of implementation than it is for nonreal-time systems.

0 At the same time these requirements are often so demanding that we must have the power of a multi-processor or application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) based implementation, so the architecture selection is a non-trivial problem that needs the support of good analysis tools.
0 Finally, the embedded systems are specialpurpose systems, whose implementation can be carefully optimized to fulfil the requirements at a minimal cost.

In this paper, we first give a brief introduction to codesign, and show how the implementation of a system is specified by the designer through the writing of a behavioural description and the selection of a hardware architecture. We then present extensions to fixed-priority scheduling theory, and derive a schedulability measurement that can be used for a heterogeneous implementation to determine how well it fulfils the performance requirements of the specification. We also provide an algorithm that calculates the optimal way of assigning task priorities in a certain implementation, and discuss how the schedulability measurement can be used as an optimization criterion in a partitioning algorithm, and for comparing different target architectures. Finally, we illustrate the whole approach by a small example.

div.head: Hardware/software codesign
div.p: The basic idea of codesign is that the behaviour of a complete system should be described abstractly in a uniform manner, regardless of in which way, hardware or software, different parts will later be realized. This behavioural description is then partitioned, by assigning the abstract entities of it to concrete parts of the physical system, and then these entities are automatically compiled into machine code (if assigned to a microprocessor), or synthesized into a circuit description. Figure l illustrates how codesign compares to the traditional system design process. The major advantages offered by codesign are: 0 A detailed specification and design is made before selecting the final hardware architecture and partitioning the system. This means that more information is available, so that these implementation decisions can be made with increased accuracy.

0 A uniform description of hardware and software components makes it less costly to move parts of the system between different partitions at later stages of development, and it also enhances the possibilities of earlier debugging and validation of the complete system.
0 Codesign moves the hardware and software development closer together, thus reducing the cost of the final integration between the technology domains.
These improvements to the design process should allow the time and cost of development to be reduced, and result in an implementation of higher quality.

div.head: System description
div.p: To be able to analyze how well a proposed system implementation meets the Liming requirements in the specification, the designer must provide a description of its behaviour, which is typically written in some higher-level programming language. h t her, we need a description of the hardware architecture which is going to be used to realize that behaviour. In addition, we must also be familiar with the functionality of the operating system, and in particular the task scheduler. In this section, we will discuss these three parts of the design, and clarify what assumptions we make about them.

div.head: Behavioural description
div.p: Common to most languages used for the programming of real-time systems, e.g. Ada, Real-Time Euclid, Erlang, is that they structure the program as a collection of concurrent tasks. Instead of limiting ourselves to one specific language, we just assume that the behavioural description P consists of a set of sporadic or periodic tasks, P = { T I , . . . , T ~} .

We demand that it is possible to analyze the worst-case timing characteristics of each task deterministically and independently. This entails that we have to disallow certain language constructs that make this analysis difficult, or even impossible. This includes: e Unbounded loops, since it is in general impossible to analytically derive bounds on the number of iterations.
0 Recursive functions, for the same reason, but also because they are very difficult to implement in silicon, and thus not very interesting from a codesign perspective.
0 Dynamic task creation, since we must have knowledge about the entire task set to be able to calculate the workload on different parts of the system.

The timing requirements are stated as deadlines D(T) for each task r E P, and to be able to analyze the system, we must also have knowledge about the periods T ( r ) (or minimum time between activations, for sporadic tasks).

div.head: Hardware architecture
div.p: One of the most interesting architecture classes for codesign is structured around a system bus that connects a shared memory to different processor nodes, i.e. microprocessors and ASICs (figure 2). We can also imagine many variations of this basic theme, e.g. by including cache memories for the microprocessors, to reduce the bus load. So when we select the hardware architecture, the range of choices we have includes: Different tasks r in the specification are statically assigned to different processor nodes, because the processors can be of different kinds, and the source code of the parts must be compiled to the machine code of the processor it is intended to run on. (For ASIC nodes, the static assignment is easier still to motivate.) pre-empts r"', or alternatively "r has higher priority than 7"'.

The operating system kernel must also be partitioned between the different processor nodes. One promising way to do that is to allocate most of the kernel in an ASIC, making the hardware responsible for inducing task switches in the software, controlling the real-time clock etc. [9]. In that way, the software part of the kernel steals virtually no processor time from the application to do administrative things.
In the next section, we will develop the necessary theory for analyzing the schedulability of a behavioural description when implemented on a heterogeneous hardware architecture.

div.head: Schedulability analysis
div.p: The goal of the codesign process for real-time systems is to find a target architecture and partitioning that allow the tasks of the behavioural description to meet their deadlines. During the iterative search for this goal, many other possible implementations will be evaluated, and to be able to guide the search in a proper direction, we must have a means of comparing the relative merits of two candidate solutions, e.g. two different target architectures or partitions. Therefore we need a continuous measurement of an implementation's quality, and in addition, we must also have a threshold value to determine if this quality is high enough to match the requirements. In the following subsections, we will derive a schedulability measurement that indicates to what degree the tasks fulfil their timing constraints.

In some situations, it might be necessary to use more complicated ways of calculating the interference than the one described above, e.g. when there are user-defined shared resources in the behavioural d e scription, which require that the access is controlled through some other protocol. div.head: Minimal required speedup
div.p: The quality of an implementation is determined by how well it meets the system's deadlines. But since we could, in theory, make any implementation meet the deadlines by simply letting it run faster, we can calculate how much faster it would at least have to be to satisfy the requirements. We call this measurement the minimal required speedup, which is denoted by S(T), and we can assert that if S(T) 5 1, meaning that no speedup at all is needed, then the deadlines will be met by the implementation.

Given a certain priority order, we can determine the minimal required speedup of a task T by calculating the value of S(T) needed for it to finish exactly on the deadline. We substitute t = D ( r ) into equation ( 1) and divide the execution time (the right-hand side) by the speedup: By isolating S ( r ) in the left-hand side, and inserting the definition of Itot(r,t) from equation (2), we obtain the formula for minimal required speedup:

For the case of a single-processor system, where I(T,T') = C(r'), Joseph and Pandya [7] have provided a pseudo-polynomial algorithm to determine if the deadlines are met by solving equation (1) as a fixed point equation. But if we instead calculate the minimal required speedup and compare it to 1, we can check the deadlines in linear time. This is due to the fact that we do not calculate the actual end-time of the task, but only whether it will finish before or after the deadline.

div.head: Priority assignment
div.p: The minimal required speedup S* of the whole task set is the maximum of the minimal speedups for each task, S* = max,.,=pS(r). Using this, we can define an optimal priority assignment to be an order < p which has a lower minimal required speedup than any other order. A more common, but looser, definition is that a priority assignment is optimal if the deadlines are reached under that order whenever they are reached under any order. This definition of optimum is compatible with ours in the sense that the deadline-monotonic priority assignment for i := 1 to m do si := c(pi); r < p r' e D ( r ) < D(r'), is optimal for the singleprocessor case with both definitions.

For the more general case with many computational resources, we have developed an optimal priorityassignment algorithm (figure 3) that has a complexity of O(m2), for m tasks, if we assume that the values of C ( r ) and 1(r, 7') are given. The algorithm tries to calculate a vector 8 = (PI,. . . , p m ) of tasks, which defines a priority order by the relation r < p r' ($ (pi = T ) A (pj = 7') A (i < j ) . Initially, this vector contains all the tasks in P in some arbitrary order, and the algorithm then works its way up from the lowest priority level to the highest, and assigns to each level the task among the remaining ones that would give the smallest required speedup at that level. The algorithm builds on the observation by Audsley et al. [l], that in order to determine the interference from higher-priority tasks, we only need to know which these tasks are, but not the priority order between them.

The vector 5 keeps the required speedups of the tasks, i.e. si = S(pi), to avoid recalculating them at each priority level, and the first for-loop of the algorithm is used to initialize the value of this vector so that it contains the speedups required at the lowest priority. The output variable S* holds the required speedup of the whole task set.

div.head: Proving the algorithm's optimality
div.p: The proof of the optimality of this algorithm is rather longish, and we therefore only give an outline of it, but the interested reader can find a complete version in [2].

It can easily be seen from the code of the algorithm, that if we swap the priorities of two tasks pi and pj, where i < j , in the priority order vector that results from the algorithm, then the new required speedup of pi will be at least as high as the old speedup of pj.

div.head: This property can be expressed formally as:
div.p: We can then prove the following lemmas about priority orders, based on this property:
1. For any priority order that does not have the property, there exists a different order that has it, but with a lower required speedup.
2. All priority orders that have the property also have equal required speedups.
So the property clearly specifies an equivalence class of optimal priority orders, and since the algorithm always returns a member of this class, it is optimal.

div.head: Partitioning
div.p: We can now use the schedulability captured by the minimal required speedup S* as a goodness criterion to be minimized during hardware/software partitioning. To find the best way to partition the system on a given architecture, we must in principle try all possible assignment combinations of different tasks to different processor nodes. If there are IC processor nodes and m tasks, we can partition in O(km) different ways, but fortunately, the problem lends itself well to a solution using a branch-and-bound algorithm, which only needs to try a few percent of all the combinations. Therefore, the designer can effectively and accurately find the optimal partitioning, and evaluate different architectures to make necessary cost/performance trade-offs at an early stage of development.

Initial experiments with the simple architecture in figure 2, with one microprocessor and one ASIC, indicate that considerable increases in schedulability are possible as a result of better partitioning. These gains are due to the fact that true parallelism is introduced at two levels: 0 A task implemented in the ASIC can run concurrently with a task in the microprocessor, as well as with other tasks in the ASIC.
0 Different parts of a task, e.g. the calculation of the two operands of a binary operator expression, can also execute in parallel when implemented in the ASIC.

The best candidates for implementation in hardware are small tasks that execute frequently, and thus consume a large share of processor time and require many context switches, and also tasks whose execution time makes it difficult to reach the deadline in software. But note that these kinds of decisions are automatically captured by the decrease in required speedup one gets by evaluating an assignment to hardware, thus we do not need to do any special classification of the task's suitability for implementation in a , certain technology (although such a classification could still be useful as a heuristic to speed up the partitioning).

But the designer should not be totally removed from this process, because sometimes it is possible to accept a suboptimal solution that has certain characteristics. An example of this was that the designer might have preferred the solution with s* = 1.2, rather than taking the more than doubled hardware cost necessary to reach S* = 1. In other situations, the user might want to influence the partitioning or the scheduling, because information exists which is difficult to capture as mathematically formulated constraints. We therefore need to deveIop took that allow the user to determine what level of automation is desired, and that let the designer step in and make certain design decisions mimually.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we have proposed a continuous measurement of schedulability-the minimal required speedup-that can be used when making design decisions in a hardware/software codesign setting. We have also presented an efficient algorithm for task priority assignment which can be used for heterogeneously implemented systems, and we have discussed how this can be coupled to an algorithm for hardwaxe/software partitioning. The scheduling technique as presented is somewhat simplified, since it uses a single fixed-priority relation throughout the entire multiprocessor system, while in reality, one might like to have different scheduling techniques for different components. We believe, however, that the techniques presented in this paper are powerful enough to allow extensions that deal with more complex assumptions, and these issues will undoubtedly be treated in the future.
